lead: A curve or a flat area rotated about an axis in its plane sweeps out a surface or a solid. The Pappus-Guldinus theorems say this sweep is simple: the swept size equals the generating length or area times the distance travelled by its centroid. Engineers use them to get paint or plating area, to estimate material for a turned part, and to find a centroid from a measured volume.
prereq: You need the centroid of a line and of an area from 4.1 and 4.2.

blocks.text: Take a plane curve of length L mm and a plane area A mm². Put an axis XX in the same plane. Let x̄ mm be the perpendicular distance from XX to the centroid of the curve or area. The axis must stay outside the shape: it may touch the boundary but must not cut the curve or the area. If it cuts, parts of the sweep land on top of each other and the count is wrong.

blocks.where: S is the swept surface area in mm²; L is the length of the generating curve in mm; x̄ is the distance from the axis to the curve centroid in mm; 2π x̄ is the path of the centroid in one full turn.

blocks.text: A full turn moves the centroid along a circle of radius x̄, so its path is 2π x̄. Multiplying this path by the curve length gives the swept surface area.

blocks.where: V is the swept volume in mm³; A is the generating plane area in mm²; x̄ is the distance from the axis to the area centroid in mm.

blocks.text: The same path times the area gives the swept volume. Both theorems assume one complete revolution. For a half turn, replace 2π by π; for an angle θ radians, replace 2π by θ.

sections.h3: From centroid to surface or volume

items: Choose the generating curve for a surface, or the generating area for a volume.
Find its centroid by 4.2 and measure x̄ perpendicular to the axis.
Check that the axis lies in the plane and does not cut the shape.
Apply S = 2π x̄ L or V = 2π x̄ A, keeping all lengths in the same unit.

blocks.text: A right circular cone shows the curve form. Its slant line has length l and centroid at its midpoint. If the base radius is r, that midpoint is r/2 from the axis. So the lateral surface is S = 2π(r/2)l = πrl.
A hemispherical shell shows the same form. A semicircular arc of radius R has length πR and centroid 2R/π from its diameter. Rotating it about that diameter gives S = 2π(2R/π)(πR) = 4πR².

The area form gives material volumes. A belt loop on a pulley rim has cross-section area A and centroid at radius x̄ from the pulley axis; its material volume is V = 2π x̄ A. A solid of revolution turned on a lathe has the same volume as the profile area swept about the spindle axis.

sections.h3: From surface or volume to centroid

blocks.text: The theorems also run backward. If a surface area S and its generating curve length L are known, the centroid distance is x̄ = S/(2πL). If a volume V and its generating area A are known, then x̄ = V/(2πA). This is useful when a part is measured or weighed and its centroid is wanted.

For a composite volume, split it into simple solids. Let Vᵢ be the volume of part i and x̄ᵢ its centroid distance from the chosen axis. The whole centroid is the weighted average x̄ = ΣVᵢx̄ᵢ / ΣVᵢ. Holes are treated as negative volumes, just as in composite areas.

items: Use a measured S with x̄ = S/(2πL) only when the sweep is one full turn.
Use a measured V with x̄ = V/(2πA) only when the axis does not cut the generating area.
Keep S in mm² and V in mm³; mixing them with cm or m changes x̄ by a factor of 10 or 1000.

figure.caption: The ring is generated by the circle; the centroid path radius R = 200 mm gives both the outer surface area and the enclosed volume.

spec.title: Two theorems, one idea
spec.aria: A circle of radius 50 mm whose centre is 200 mm from the axis sweeps a surface of area 394784.18 mm² and a volume of 9869604.40 mm³.

examples.question: A ring of circular cross-section is made by revolving a circle of radius 50 mm whose centre is 200 mm from the axis. Find the surface area and the volume.
steps: The generating curve is the circle perimeter. L = 2πr = 2π × 50 = 314.16 mm. Its centroid is the circle centre, so x̄ = 200 mm. The axis does not cut the circle because 200 mm > 50 mm.
Surface area: S = 2π x̄ L = 2π × 200 × 314.16 = 394784.18 mm². In square metres this is 0.394784 m².
The generating area is the disk. A = πr² = π × 50² = 7853.98 mm². Its centroid is again x̄ = 200 mm from the axis.
Volume: V = 2π x̄ A = 2π × 200 × 7853.98 = 9869604.40 mm³. In powers of ten this is 9.869604 × 10⁶ mm³.
examples.answer: Surface area = 394784.18 mm² and volume = 9869604.40 mm³.
examples.check:
import math
r = 50.0
R = 200.0
L = 2 * math.pi * r
S = 2 * math.pi * R * L
A = math.pi * r**2
V = 2 * math.pi * R * A
print(f"{S:.2f}")
print(f"{V:.2f}")

traps: Using the distance from the axis to the nearest edge instead of to the centroid. For the ring, the edge distances are 150 mm and 250 mm, not 200 mm.
Applying the theorem when the axis cuts the area or curve. The swept parts overlap, so 2π x̄ A or 2π x̄ L no longer counts distinct material.
Dropping the 2 in 2π. One full revolution is 2π x̄, not π x̄; π x̄ is a half turn.
Mixing the two formulas: using curve length L in the volume formula, or area A in the surface formula.
For a cone, using l/2 as x̄ instead of r/2. The centroid of the slant line is r/2 from the axis, where r is the base radius.

quiz.q: State the two Pappus-Guldinus theorems with their formulas.
quiz.a: Surface area S = 2π x̄ L, where L is the generating curve length and x̄ is the distance of its centroid from the axis. Volume V = 2π x̄ A, where A is the generating area and x̄ is the distance of its centroid from the axis.

quiz.q: Why must the axis not cut the generating curve or area?
quiz.a: If the axis cuts the shape, the sweep overlaps itself. The formulas count every part once, so overlapping parts would be counted more than once and the surface area or volume would be wrong.

quiz.q: A semicircular arc of radius 30 mm is rotated about its diameter. Find the surface area.
A right circular cone has base radius 40 mm and slant length 100 mm. Use Pappus-Guldinus to find its lateral surface area.
quiz.a: The slant line has length L = 100 mm. Its centroid is r/2 = 20 mm from the axis. S = 2π × 20 × 100 = 12566.37 mm².

quiz.q: A rectangle 40 mm by 10 mm is rotated about an external axis parallel to its 40 mm side. The centroid is 30 mm from the axis. Find the volume swept.
For the ring with r = 50 mm and centroid distance 200 mm, a student uses 250 mm as x̄. Find the percentage error in S and V.
quiz.a: Both S and V are proportional to x̄. The ratio is 250/200 = 1.25, so both answers are 25% too large.

quiz.q: A turned solid has measured volume 2.0 × 10⁶ mm³ and its generating profile area is 5000 mm². Find the centroid distance from the axis.
quiz.a: x̄ = V/(2πA) = 2.0 × 10⁶/(2π × 5000) = 63.66 mm. This assumes one full revolution and an axis that does not cut the profile.

beyond: Not for the exam. CAD packages compute mass properties by sweeping profiles and summing moments, and the Pappus relations are the hand check. In shell theory, the same centroid-path idea gives surface areas of domes and pressure vessels. In manufacturing, lathe and additive profiles are sized from swept volumes. Search for "Pappus centroid theorem", "surface of revolution area", and "solid of revolution volume".
